concept.name: Daily loss limit
concept.definition: A risk control that stops or restricts trading for the rest of the day once cumulative losses — realized plus, in strict versions, floating P/L on open positions — reach a predetermined amount, typically a fixed sum or a percentage of equity.
concept.intuition: It is the circuit breaker for a bad day: cap the damage a single session can do and force the trader to step away before tilt and revenge trading compound the loss.
concept.mechanics: Track day P/L against the limit; on breach, flatten positions and/or block new orders until the next session. Prop-firm variants compute the limit from a daily reference balance — e.g. FTMO: previous midnight balance minus 5% of initial capital, checked continuously against equity including open positions, commissions, and swaps.
concept.formula: Breach if equity_t < reference_balance_day - L_daily, where L_daily is the daily loss allowance (e.g. 5% of initial capital) and equity includes floating P/L, commissions, and swaps.
concept.failure_modes: Gaps and illiquidity can push losses well beyond the limit before positions can be closed, and limit-aware traders may size up recklessly early in the day or hoard risk into the reset. A daily cap does not bound total drawdown, which accumulates across many within-limit days.
concept.misconceptions: The limit is usually measured on equity, not closed balance — open floating losses count in real time — and it resets against the latest reference balance, so the floor moves day to day rather than staying fixed.
concept.example: On a $200,000 evaluation account with a 5% maximum daily loss, equity may never fall below $190,000 on day one; if the midnight balance rises to $204,000, the next day's floor moves to $194,000.
